public_statements.boeing:
We said we would turn this big ship, and I think we've turned it. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and MAX 10 are certified, and our balance sheet is back where it belongs. That is the work of a lot of people doing it the right way, and the financials followed our production performance.

It doesn't change how we run the place. The 737 line stays on the plan we've laid out, and the KPIs tell us when we're ready, not the calendar. We'll keep building 787 capacity in Charleston, because customers want more of that airplane and we intend to keep it the most efficient in its segment.

On a new airplane, our thinking hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. When we do, it will be planned around a stable supply of parts, starting with engines, and more than one engine source. I'm not going to give a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, we'll set the schedule with headroom in it, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s, and we plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. We are inviting all three narrowbody engine makers, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, to power it. A stable, diversified engine supply is a condition of a disciplined and controlled ramp-up and of serving our customers well. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: we will keep its lines running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We will take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we will keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we will recruit and train, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build this aircraft.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. Our customers fly LEAP and GEnx today, and our job is to deliver those engines and keep them on wing. LEAP durability upgrades are going into new engines and, through the shops, into the fleet. On the 787 we're upgrading the GEnx, because our airline customers make their money on time on wing, and so do we.

Here's what we don't know: when the next narrowbody will be launched, and by whom. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. CFM, with our partners at Safran, will be ready to support every airframer that moves, with a LEAP derivative or with a new engine. CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: I'll start with the bad news. For years the GTF fleet was not where our customers needed it to be. We own that, and we have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. So we control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch. It will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life, and time on wing, not just fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. It comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. For the fleet flying today, the GTF Hot Section kit is available at shop visit on standard terms, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. When we've seen the demand and we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. Our route into the narrowbody is a partnership, not a solo programme: Rolls-Royce stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology we bring. We take a narrowbody engine forward only for an airframe that has chosen it. Entry into service will be no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation, with in-service support through partner shops in place before entry into service. We don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
public_statements.embraer: Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We focused on delivering the results in our plan to 2030 with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. We keep doing that, with a very healthy cash generation to support a potential next move. On a new product, I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies because it is important that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. We need a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. Any large investment will be made with partners, and we talk to many partners and to all the engine makers. Today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. This does not depend only on us. It depends on the technology available in the market and on the partners, and the investment has to prove its return. On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions, and I can only speak for Embraer. On trade, Embraer is about engineering, and we focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic. We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost.

public_statements.boeing:
We said we'd get the basics right first, and the team has done that. The 777X is delivering, the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and we've paid the debt down to where we wanted it. I think we've turned the ship. The job now is to keep it pointed the right way.

On the 737, we're staying at 57 a month. Our KPIs are stable, and that rate serves the demand we see. We'll move the rate when the demand and the data say so, and not before.

On widebodies, the 777X is in service and the 787 line is stable at Charleston. We're going to keep both of those lines running the way they are now.

On a new single-aisle airplane, we're doing the work on the market, the technology and our own readiness. We'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're not there yet, and I'm not going to give you a date. When we do it, we want more than one engine source on that airplane. That's a requirement, and we're working on it with the engine makers.

It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do, and they frame today's decision. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is planned to enter service in the second half of the 2030s. The date follows a technology and production system we have matured over the past decade, and we set it on our own clock.

We are preparing the Airbus of the 2030s while we keep delivering for our customers today. The A320 family stays at its present rate until the new aircraft enters service. Our production plan then keeps A320 lines running longer through the new aircraft's ramp-up, so that the transition is disciplined and controlled, rate by rate, with quality first. We have asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the aircraft, and we will certify them in sequence as each one matures.

The programme is funded within our cash flow and preserves our financial flexibility and balance-sheet discipline; the case assumes no state support. We are securing our own supply base, from work packages to materials, and investing in the people who will design and build this aircraft. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aerospace. We will report progress against milestones, in windows, as the aircraft matures.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we'll run this business through the next decade.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: our customers fly more LEAP and GEnx hours every year, and job one is keeping those engines on wing longer. So we keep putting durability upgrades into the LEAP fleet, and we're upgrading the GEnx for the 787 operators who count on it.

What we don't know is when the next single-aisle airplanes come. It's really not for us to say. That's the airframers' call, shaped by the airlines. When they decide, CFM will be there for both of them, with the engine their airplane needs, LEAP-based or new, on a date our testing backs. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We'll earn it.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with our partner Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan would not enter service before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
The bad news first. The GTF fleet still has work ahead of it, and that work comes before anything new: time on wing, parts, and getting our customers' aircraft back in the air. We are putting the GTF Advantage hot section into the fleet at shop visits, and we will keep doing it until the fleet is where it needs to be. Control what you can control.

Here is our commitment on the next engine. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it. It will be ready six years from launch, which means 2036 if it is launched this year. Durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one. GTF2 builds on the gear and the GTF Advantage core that are flying today. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it.

We will compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates, and we will not get out ahead of them. When we've seen the demand and when we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, our position is simple. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. We don't commit that easily: until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing. Our preference is partnership. The Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney on terms that credit the technology we bring, and we will commit once they do. Widebody is our core, and our focus there stays on time on wing. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

One more correction, on engines. When we do launch, the airplane will carry more than one engine source, from engines that are ready when the airplane is. That's the requirement. I'm not going to name makers today, and the entry-into-service date will have headroom built in.
